q: Under New York's statute of frauds, which agreement must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged to be enforceable?
options: A lease of an apartment for six months
An agreement for a salesperson to show a home on Saturday
A contract for the sale of a single-family house
A month-to-month rental of a garage space
explanation: GOL § 5-703 requires contracts for the sale of real property (and leases longer than one year) to be in a writing subscribed by the party to be charged. Leases of one year or less, like a six-month or month-to-month rental, may be oral.

q: Before the tenant moves in, a landlord and tenant orally agree to a two-year lease of a store. The landlord then refuses to honor it. The oral lease is best described as:
options: Unenforceable, because a lease for more than one year must be in writing
Void, because a lease can never be created orally
Fully enforceable, because both parties clearly agreed to it
Voidable only at the tenant's option because the tenant relied on it
explanation: A lease for more than one year falls within the statute of frauds, so this oral two-year lease cannot be enforced in court. Trap: it is unenforceable, not void — oral leases of one year or less are perfectly valid.

q: Which of the following is NOT an essential element of a valid real estate contract?
options: Competent parties who have legal capacity to contract
Consideration exchanged between the buyer and seller
A lawful object or purpose for the agreement
Recording in the county clerk's office
explanation: A valid contract needs competent parties, mutual assent (offer and acceptance), consideration, and a lawful object, and a real estate sale contract must also be in writing. Recording gives constructive notice to the public; it is not required for the contract to be valid between the parties.
citation: General contract law; NY GOL § 5-703; NY RPL § 291 (recording)

q: A 17-year-old signs a contract to buy a vacant lot from an adult seller. The contract is:
options: Void from the start because minors cannot sign contracts
Voidable at the minor's option
Voidable at the seller's option only
Valid and binding on both parties because both signed
explanation: In New York a person under 18 is a minor (infant). A minor's contract is generally voidable by the minor, who may disaffirm it, while the adult remains bound if the minor chooses to go through with it. Trap: voidable, not void.

q: Two parties sign a contract whose stated purpose is to sell a building to be used for an illegal gambling operation. The contract is:
options: Void, because it lacks a lawful object
Voidable at the buyer's option
Valid but unenforceable until the buyer obtains a license
Valid, because transferring real property is itself legal
explanation: A contract for an illegal purpose lacks the essential element of a lawful object, so it is void — it has no legal effect, and neither party can enforce it. Voidable contracts (such as those induced by fraud or a minor's contract) are valid until one party disaffirms.

q: A buyer and a seller sign a written purchase contract in which the buyer promises to pay $410,000 and the seller promises to convey title. This contract is best described as:
options: Implied and unilateral
Express and unilateral
Express and bilateral
Implied and bilateral
explanation: It is express because the terms are stated in words (written or oral), and bilateral because each side exchanges a promise for a promise. An implied contract arises from conduct, and a unilateral contract is a promise given in exchange for an act.

q: A seller tells area brokers she will pay a $5,000 bonus to whichever cooperating agent first brings a buyer who closes. No agent promises to do anything. This arrangement is best described as:
options: A bilateral contract binding on every broker who hears it
An executed contract as soon as it is announced
A void contract for lack of any consideration
A unilateral contract, accepted only by performance
explanation: A unilateral contract is a promise in exchange for an act: only the seller is bound, and an agent accepts by actually producing the buyer who closes. No agent is obligated to try, which is why it is not bilateral.

q: A purchase contract has been signed by both buyer and seller, and the closing is scheduled for next month. Right now the contract is:
options: Executed, because both parties have signed it
Executory, because performance is still to come
Unilateral, because only the seller still has to act
Implied, because the closing terms are still pending
explanation: An executory contract has obligations still to be performed; it becomes executed only when both sides have fully performed (here, at closing). Trap: 'executed' does not mean 'signed.'

q: A buyer offers $500,000. The seller replies, 'I'll take $520,000.' The buyer declines. The next day the seller says, 'Fine, I accept your $500,000 offer.' What is the legal status?
options: No contract yet; the seller's statement is only a new offer the buyer may accept or reject
A binding contract at $500,000, because the seller accepted the buyer's exact original terms
A binding contract at $520,000, because that was the last price either party stated
A binding contract at $500,000, but the buyer may cancel within three days of the acceptance
explanation: A counteroffer is a rejection of the original offer and terminates it. The buyer's $500,000 offer no longer exists to be accepted, so the seller's later 'acceptance' is only a new offer that the buyer is free to accept or reject.

q: A buyer hands a salesperson a $20,000 earnest money check payable to the brokerage. What should the salesperson do?
options: Deposit it in the salesperson's own personal account and hold it there until closing
Keep it safely in a locked desk drawer at the office until the closing date is near
Promptly turn it over to the supervising broker for deposit in a separate escrow account
Give it directly to the seller, since the earnest money belongs to the seller once signed
explanation: A salesperson must promptly turn over funds belonging to others to the supervising broker, who must keep them in a separate special (escrow) account. Mixing client money with personal or business money is commingling, and using it is conversion — both are prohibited.

q: A buyer signs a binding purchase contract with no remaining contingencies, then changes her mind and refuses to close. She demands her earnest money back. Generally:
options: She is automatically entitled to a full refund because the deal never actually closed
The broker must refund it to her within 30 days, as required by the license law
The broker may keep the full deposit as its earned commission on the failed sale
No automatic refund; the contract's default terms decide who gets the deposit
explanation: An earnest-money refund is not automatic just because the buyer changes her mind. Once contingencies are satisfied or have expired, the contract's default and liquidated damages terms decide who gets the deposit. The broker holds it in trust and cannot simply keep it as a commission.

q: A contract's mortgage contingency gives the buyer until June 1 to get a loan commitment. The buyer applies promptly and in good faith but is denied, and gives the seller written notice on May 25 as the contract requires. The buyer most likely may:
options: Be forced to close with cash because loan denial is the buyer's risk
Cancel the contract and recover the deposit under the contingency
Cancel only if the seller agrees to waive the deadline
Keep the contract alive indefinitely until some loan is approved
explanation: A mortgage contingency lets a buyer who makes a good-faith application and is denied cancel and get the deposit back, as long as the buyer follows the clause's notice and deadline terms. Missing the deadline or not applying in good faith can lose that protection.

q: An upstate contract filled out by a salesperson has an attorney approval clause with a three-business-day review period. Neither party's attorney sends written disapproval within the period. What is the result?
options: The contingency is deemed waived and the contract is binding
The contract automatically terminates for lack of approval
The salesperson's broker must approve the contract instead
The parties automatically get 30 more days to obtain approval
explanation: A standard attorney approval clause says the contingency is deemed waived unless an attorney sends written disapproval by the deadline. The clause lets licensees fill in a form contract without engaging in the unauthorized practice of law, while still giving each side's attorney a chance to review it.
citation: NY Judiciary Law § 478 (unauthorized practice of law); standard attorney-approval clause

q: A contract says that if the buyer defaults, the seller may keep the buyer's 10% down payment as the seller's sole remedy. This provision is a(n):
options: Specific performance clause
Rescission clause
Liquidated damages clause
Acceleration clause
explanation: Liquidated damages are an amount the parties agree to in advance as compensation for a breach — often the earnest money. Specific performance forces completion of the sale, rescission cancels the contract and restores both parties, and acceleration is a mortgage clause.

q: A seller signs a valid sale contract, then refuses to close because she got a higher offer. The buyer wants the property itself, not money. The buyer should sue for:
options: Liquidated damages
Rescission
A deficiency judgment
Specific performance
explanation: Specific performance is an equitable remedy in which a court orders the breaching party to perform. Courts grant it in real estate cases because every parcel is unique. Rescission would cancel the deal, which is the opposite of what this buyer wants.

q: After signing, a buyer discovers the seller knowingly lied about the house being connected to public sewer. The buyer wants to cancel and put both parties back where they were before the contract, including return of the deposit. This remedy is:
options: Specific performance
Rescission
Novation
Liquidated damages
explanation: Fraud or misrepresentation makes a contract voidable by the injured party, who may seek rescission: the contract is canceled and each party is restored to its pre-contract position. Novation substitutes a new contract or party; it does not unwind the deal.

q: Under an exclusive right to sell listing, the owner finds a buyer on her own (a coworker) and sells during the listing term without the broker's help. The broker is:
options: Entitled to the commission, because the broker is paid no matter who sells
Not entitled to anything, because the owner found the buyer herself
Entitled to half the commission by law
Entitled only to reimbursement of advertising costs
explanation: Under an exclusive right to sell, the listing broker earns the agreed commission if the property sells during the term, no matter who finds the buyer — including the owner. That is the key difference from an exclusive agency listing.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an exclusive agency listing from an exclusive right to sell listing?
options: Under exclusive agency, the broker is paid even if the owner sells on her own
Exclusive agency lets the owner list with several brokers at the same time
Exclusive agency must be oral, while exclusive right to sell must be written
Under exclusive agency, the owner owes no commission if she finds the buyer herself
explanation: Exclusive agency names one broker but reserves the owner's right to sell on her own without owing a commission; under exclusive right to sell, the broker is paid regardless. Listing with several brokers at once is an open listing. NY regulations require exclusive listing agreements to include an explanation of this difference.

q: An owner gives open listings to three brokers. Broker B is the procuring cause of the sale. Who earns a commission?
options: All three brokers, split equally
The first broker who signed a listing
Only Broker B
No broker, because open listings cannot be enforced
explanation: In an open listing, only the broker who is the procuring cause of the sale earns the commission. If the owner sells the property herself, she owes no one.

q: A tenant's lease gives the tenant a right of first refusal to buy the building. Which statement is correct?
options: The tenant can force the landlord to sell at a set price at any time during the lease
The tenant can match a bona fide offer the landlord is willing to accept, but cannot force a sale
The tenant is obligated to buy the building if the landlord decides to sell
A right of first refusal and an option to purchase are the same thing
explanation: A right of first refusal only lets the holder match terms if the owner decides to sell; it cannot force a sale. An option, by contrast, lets the optionee (who pays consideration) compel the sale at a set price within the option period — the optionor is bound, the optionee is not.
citation: General contract law (options and rights of first refusal)

q: A buyer assigns her purchase contract to her brother with the seller's consent, but no agreement releasing the buyer is signed. If the brother fails to close:
options: The original buyer is automatically released because the seller consented
The seller can sue only the brokerage
The contract is void because real estate contracts cannot be assigned
The original buyer generally remains liable, because only a novation releases her
explanation: In an assignment, the assignor generally stays secondarily liable if the assignee does not perform. A novation replaces the old contract or party with a new one and releases the original party. Consenting to an assignment is not the same as agreeing to a release.

q: In parts of downstate New York, a licensee may prepare a binder. Which statement about a binder is most accurate?
options: A written outline of key terms that can be enforceable if it contains all essential terms
It is the title insurance policy that the title company delivers to the buyer at closing
It can never be enforced, because only a contract prepared by an attorney is binding
It replaces the deed and transfers title to the buyer once all parties have signed it
explanation: A binder is a written outline of the main terms, often signed by the parties, after which attorneys draft the formal contract of sale. A binder may lack essential terms such as contingencies, but one that has all the required elements can be an enforceable contract.

q: Under contract law, the element that exists when one party's offer is accepted on exactly its terms is usually called:
options: Mutual assent, or a meeting of the minds
Consideration, or a bargained-for exchange
Legal capacity of both parties
Legality of the contract's object
explanation: Offer plus unqualified acceptance produces mutual assent (a meeting of the minds). Consideration is a separate element: the exchange of value, not the agreement itself.

q: A seller's listing advertises her house 'for $600,000.' A buyer emails the listing agent, 'I accept your $600,000 price.' The seller has signed nothing further. Generally:
options: A contract exists, because the buyer accepted the exact advertised price
A contract exists once the listing agent receives the buyer's email
No contract exists, because an advertised price is an invitation to negotiate
A contract exists, but only the buyer can enforce it against the seller
explanation: Advertisements and listing prices invite offers; they are not offers that can be accepted. The buyer's email is itself an offer, and the seller is free to accept, counter, or reject it.

q: A buyer signed an installment land contract at age 17. After turning 18, she kept making the monthly payments for two years without objecting. The contract is most likely:
options: Still voidable at her option at any time she chooses
Void, because she lacked capacity when she signed it
Ratified by her conduct and now binding on her
Unenforceable until a court approves the original signing
explanation: A minor's contract is voidable, but continuing to perform for a substantial time after reaching majority (18 in New York) ratifies it. The 'void' trap confuses a minor's contract with one lacking any legal effect.

q: A 16-year-old and an adult sign a contract under which the minor will buy the adult's vacant lot. Before closing, the adult changes his mind. Which statement is correct?
options: Either party may disaffirm because the contract is void
The adult may disaffirm at any time before the closing
Neither party may disaffirm once both have signed
The adult is bound; only the minor may disaffirm
explanation: Voidability protects the minor only: the minor may disaffirm, but the adult party stays bound. Calling the contract void is the trap; it is voidable, and only at the minor's option.

q: Which of the following contracts is generally VOID rather than merely voidable?
options: One signed by a 17-year-old buyer of a building lot
One the buyer signed after the seller's fraudulent statement
One signed by a person a court had already declared incompetent
One a seller signed while too intoxicated to understand it
explanation: Under the traditional rule, a contract made by someone already adjudicated incompetent is void. Minority, fraud, and intoxication make a contract voidable by the protected party, so it stays valid unless that party chooses to avoid it.

q: At a party, a seller signs a sale contract while so intoxicated that he cannot understand what he is signing. When sober the next morning, he promptly objects. The contract is most likely:
options: Void from the start for both parties
Valid, since he chose to drink
Voidable by the buyer only
Voidable by the seller
explanation: Intoxication severe enough to prevent understanding makes a contract voidable by the impaired party, who must act promptly once sober. It is not automatically void, and the sober buyer has no right to avoid it.

q: Each of the following ends an offer EXCEPT:
options: The offeror's death before any acceptance
A counteroffer made by the offeree
The passing of the offer's stated deadline
The offeree asking whether the price is firm
explanation: A mere inquiry about the terms does not reject or change the offer, so the offer survives. Death of the offeror, a counteroffer (which acts as a rejection), and lapse of time all terminate an offer.

q: A buyer offers $475,000 with a June 30 closing. The seller signs the offer but crosses out 'June 30,' writes 'July 15,' and initials the change. The seller has made:
options: A counteroffer that the buyer may accept or reject
A binding acceptance, because the change is minor
A binding acceptance on the original June 30 date
An acceptance that binds unless the buyer objects
explanation: Acceptance must match the offer exactly; changing any term, even a closing date, is a counteroffer that rejects the original offer. No contract exists until the buyer accepts the July 15 date.

q: Under the mailbox rule, an acceptance sent by a method the offer authorizes is generally effective when it is:
options: Received by the offeror
Sent by the offeree
Read by the offeror
Acknowledged by the offeror
explanation: The mailbox (dispatch) rule makes a properly sent acceptance effective on dispatch, even before it arrives. Receipt is the rule for revocations, which is the usual trap.

q: A seller mails a revocation of her offer on Monday. The buyer, who has not heard anything, mails an acceptance on Tuesday. The buyer receives the revocation Wednesday, and the seller receives the acceptance Thursday. Generally:
options: A contract was formed Tuesday, when the acceptance was mailed
No contract exists, because the revocation was mailed first
No contract exists, because the revocation arrived Wednesday
A contract was formed Thursday, when the acceptance arrived
explanation: A revocation is effective only when received (Wednesday), but an acceptance is effective when dispatched (Tuesday). The acceptance took effect first, so the contract was formed Tuesday.

q: An offer states, 'Your acceptance is effective only when I actually receive your signed copy.' The buyer mails the signed copy Monday; it arrives Friday. On Wednesday the offeror phones the buyer and revokes. Generally:
options: A contract was formed Monday, when the buyer mailed the signed copy
No contract, since the offer required receipt and the revocation came first
A contract was formed Friday, when the signed copy reached the offeror
No contract, because a written offer cannot be revoked by telephone
explanation: The offeror controls the offer and may require receipt, displacing the dispatch rule. The Wednesday revocation reached the buyer before the acceptance reached the offeror, so the offer was gone when it arrived.

q: Unless an offer has been made irrevocable (for example, by a paid option), an offeror may generally revoke it:
options: Only after giving the offeree 24 hours' notice
Only if the offer contained a stated deadline
At any time up until the scheduled closing
At any time before the acceptance takes effect
explanation: An ordinary offer can be withdrawn any time before acceptance becomes effective. Once acceptance takes effect a contract exists, so revoking afterward (up to closing) would be a breach, not a revocation.

q: A buyer pays an owner $5,000 for the right to buy his land for $300,000 at any time within 90 days. On day 30, the owner announces he is withdrawing the offer. The owner:
options: May withdraw if he returns the buyer's $5,000 payment
Cannot withdraw; the paid option holds the offer open for 90 days
May withdraw, because the buyer has not yet agreed to buy
May withdraw with written notice, since options are revocable
explanation: Because the buyer gave consideration for the promise to keep the offer open, the option is a binding contract for its 90-day term. Refunding the money does not undo the bargain the owner already made.

q: A buyer's offer says, 'If I don't hear from you by Friday, I'll treat your silence as acceptance.' The seller never responds. Generally:
options: No contract exists, because silence is ordinarily not acceptance
A contract formed Friday when the stated deadline passed
A contract formed, but only the buyer is bound by it
A contract formed once the buyer deposited earnest money
explanation: An offeror cannot force a contract on the offeree by declaring that silence will count as acceptance. Acceptance requires some words or conduct showing assent.

q: In contract law, consideration is best defined as:
options: Something of legal value each party bargains for and gives
The earnest money the buyer deposits when the contract is signed
The fair market value of the property that is being sold
The written terms that both parties have read and signed
explanation: Consideration is the bargained-for exchange of legal value: money, property, a promise, or forbearance. A deposit is one common form, but exchanged promises alone can be enough.

q: A lender promises not to start foreclosure for 60 days in exchange for the borrower's promise to pay a $1,000 fee. The lender's agreement to refrain from exercising a legal right is called:
options: Forbearance
Novation
Laches
Ratification
explanation: Forbearance (giving up or delaying a legal right) is valid consideration. Novation substitutes a new contract or party, and laches is an equitable defense based on delay.

q: All winter, without being asked, a neighbor clears snow from an owner's driveway. In the spring the owner orally promises to pay him $500, then refuses. The oral promise is generally:
options: Enforceable, because the work had real value to the owner
Enforceable as an implied contract for the past work
Voidable at the neighbor's option for lack of a writing
Unenforceable, because past acts are not consideration
explanation: Consideration must be bargained for at the time of the promise; services already given freely are past consideration. New York's GOL §5-1105 can save such a promise only if it is in a signed writing that states the past consideration, and this one was oral.

q: To get a buyer to sign, a seller covers a cracked foundation wall with paneling and denies any structural problems when asked. The buyer signs. The contract is:
options: Voidable at the buyer's option
Void from the very beginning
Voidable at either party's option
Valid, because the buyer could inspect
explanation: Fraud impairs the deceived party's consent, so the buyer may affirm or avoid the contract. It is not void, and the seller who committed the fraud cannot use it to escape.

q: In a contract-classification question, an executed contract is one that:
options: Both parties have finished signing
Both parties have fully performed
Has been recorded with the county
Both attorneys have approved in writing
explanation: In classification, 'executed' means fully performed, while 'executory' means performance remains. In everyday use 'executed' also means signed, which is the trap: a signed purchase contract is still executory until closing.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a bilateral contract from a unilateral contract?
options: Bilateral contracts need a writing, while unilateral ones may be oral
Bilateral contracts bind both parties only after the closing occurs
Bilateral binds two parties; unilateral binds only one party's heirs
Bilateral trades a promise for a promise; unilateral trades a promise for an act
explanation: In a bilateral contract both sides promise. In a unilateral contract one side promises and the other accepts only by performing the requested act.

q: A seller signs a written sale contract, but the buyer never signs it. Under New York's statute of frauds, which statement is correct?
options: Neither party can enforce it unless both have signed
The seller could enforce it against the buyer, but not the reverse
The buyer could enforce it against the seller, but not the reverse
Both parties can enforce it because the terms are in writing
explanation: GOL §5-703 requires the signature of the party to be charged, meaning the party being sued. The seller signed, so the contract can be enforced against the seller; the buyer did not sign, so it cannot be enforced against the buyer.

q: A landlord and tenant orally agree to a one-year lease of an apartment beginning today. Under GOL §5-703, the oral lease is:
options: Unenforceable, because every real property lease must be in writing
Void, because a lease is a conveyance that must be recorded
Potentially enforceable, since only leases longer than one year need a writing
Enforceable only if the tenant has paid a security deposit
explanation: The statute of frauds reaches leases for longer than one year; a one-year lease starting immediately can be oral. A lease longer than one year would need a signed writing.

q: Under GOL §5-703, when an agent signs a real estate sale contract on a principal's behalf, the agent's authority to sign must be:
options: Given in writing
Given orally before a witness
Recorded with the county clerk
Approved by the Department of State
explanation: The statute requires the writing to be signed by the party to be charged or by a lawful agent authorized in writing. Oral authority does not satisfy it.

q: Under an oral agreement to buy a house, a buyer moved in with the seller's consent, paid most of the price, and built an addition. The seller now refuses to deliver a deed. The buyer's strongest argument is that:
options: Oral land contracts are void, but she has acquired title through adverse possession
Oral contracts for land become enforceable once six years have passed
Part performance may let a court order specific performance despite the lack of a writing
The parol evidence rule makes the oral terms binding against the seller
explanation: GOL §5-703(4) preserves a court's power to compel specific performance where part performance (such as possession plus improvements) is unequivocally referable to the oral agreement. Adverse possession fails because her possession was with the seller's permission, not hostile.

q: In New York, the general statute of limitations for an action for breach of contract is:
options: Three years
Ten years
Six years
Two years
explanation: CPLR §213 gives six years for contract actions. Ten years is New York's adverse possession period, a common mix-up.

q: A seller breached a purchase contract on April 15, 2022. Under New York's general limitations period for contract actions, the buyer's time to sue runs out on about:
options: April 15, 2025
April 15, 2032
April 15, 2028
April 15, 2024
explanation: Contract actions have a six-year period: 2022 + 6 = 2028. The distractors apply 3, 10, or 2 years instead.

q: A buyer waits many months to seek specific performance, and in the meantime the seller makes costly changes in reliance on the deal being dead. The equitable defense based on this unreasonable, prejudicial delay is:
options: The statute of limitations
Laches
The statute of frauds
The parol evidence rule
explanation: Laches bars equitable relief when unreasonable delay prejudices the other side, even within the statutory deadline. The statute of limitations is a fixed time bar, and the statute of frauds concerns writings.

q: The parol evidence rule generally prevents a party from:
options: Using earlier oral statements to contradict a complete written contract
Enforcing any oral agreement that involves an interest in real property
Introducing any evidence of fraud or duress during a lawsuit
Amending a written contract in any way after it has been signed
explanation: Once the parties adopt a final, complete writing, prior or contemporaneous oral agreements cannot change its terms. The rule does not bar proof of fraud or later modifications; the writing requirement for land is the statute of frauds.

q: A signed final contract with a merger clause says the sale includes all kitchen appliances. The seller claims that before signing, the buyer orally agreed she could take the refrigerator. A court will most likely:
options: Let the seller take the refrigerator based on the oral deal
Follow the writing, so the refrigerator stays with the house
Void the contract because the parties now disagree
Split the refrigerator's value between the two parties
explanation: The merger clause shows the writing is the parties' complete agreement, so the parol evidence rule excludes the earlier oral side deal that contradicts it.

q: Despite the parol evidence rule, which of the following may generally be proved with evidence outside a complete written contract?
options: That the parties orally agreed to a lower price
That an earlier oral deal added a missing term
That the parties orally agreed to a later closing
That the buyer was tricked into signing by fraud
explanation: The rule bars prior or contemporaneous oral terms that vary the writing, but evidence of fraud, duress, or mistake is admissible because it attacks whether a valid contract was formed at all.

q: Obtaining a party's signature on a contract by threatening physical harm is:
options: Undue influence
Misrepresentation
Forbearance
Duress
explanation: Duress is coercion through threats, and it makes the contract voidable by the victim. Undue influence instead involves abusing a relationship of trust, without threats.

q: An elderly owner relies on her live-in caregiver for every decision. The caregiver persuades her to sell him her house for half its value. Her best ground to avoid the sale is:
options: Duress
Mutual mistake
Lack of consideration
Undue influence
explanation: Undue influence is unfair persuasion by someone in a position of trust or dominance, and it makes the contract voidable. There was no threat (duress), and half the value is still consideration.

q: A buyer wants to cancel because the seller called the house 'the nicest home on the block,' and the buyer now disagrees. Generally the buyer:
options: Can cancel for fraud, because the claim proved untrue
Can cancel for mutual mistake about the home's quality
Cannot cancel, because the remark is opinion (puffing)
Can cancel, because the statement was made orally
explanation: Fraud requires a false statement of material fact. Vague praise and opinion (puffing) are not statements of fact the buyer may justifiably rely on.

q: Unknown to both parties, the lakeside cottage being sold burned down the day before they signed the contract. The doctrine that best allows the buyer to avoid the contract is:
options: Unilateral mistake about value
Undue influence by the seller
Laches
Mutual mistake of a material fact
explanation: Both parties shared a mistaken belief about a basic fact (the cottage existed), which allows the contract to be avoided. A unilateral mistake about value generally gives no relief.

q: A buyer signs believing the house will gain 20% in value within a year. Prices stay flat, and she wants out before closing. Generally she:
options: May rescind for mutual mistake about the home's value
Is still bound, since a wrong value prediction is no defense
May rescind for fraud, since the seller gave no warning
May rescind because the contract is still executory
explanation: A party's mistaken prediction about future value is a business risk, not a mistake of existing fact, and nobody misrepresented anything. An executory contract is still binding.

q: Specific performance is generally available to enforce real estate sale contracts mainly because:
options: Money damages are not allowed in real estate cases
The statute of frauds requires that remedy
Each parcel of land is considered unique
Brokers must be paid at the closing table
explanation: Because no two parcels are identical, money may not adequately replace the bargained-for property, so courts may order the breaching party to convey it. Money damages remain available as an alternative.

q: A buyer breaches a $450,000 purchase contract that has no liquidated damages clause. The seller promptly resells for $420,000 and incurs $6,000 in extra carrying costs from the delay. The seller's compensatory damages are most likely:
explanation: Damages = ($450,000 − $420,000) + $6,000 = $30,000 + $6,000 = $36,000. $30,000 omits the carrying costs, $24,000 subtracts them, and $45,000 is merely a 10% deposit figure.

q: A $385,000 contract requires a 10% down payment and says the seller keeps it as liquidated damages if the buyer defaults. The buyer defaults without legal excuse, and the seller later resells for $400,000. The seller may generally keep:
options: $38,500, the full down payment
$0, since the resale price was higher
$23,500, the deposit minus the resale gain
$19,250, half of the down payment
explanation: Down payment = 10% × $385,000 = $38,500. New York courts generally let a seller keep a down payment of up to 10% when the buyer defaults without lawful excuse, even if the seller later resells at a profit ($400,000 − $385,000 = $15,000 is not deducted).
citation: General contract law (liquidated damages); Maxton Builders, Inc. v. Lo Galbo, 68 N.Y.2d 373 (1986)

q: A court will generally refuse to enforce a liquidated damages clause when the stated amount:
options: Is grossly out of proportion to any likely loss
Equals 10% of the contract purchase price
Was agreed upon before any breach occurred
Is stated as a fixed dollar figure
explanation: Liquidated damages must be a reasonable estimate of hard-to-measure losses fixed in advance. A grossly disproportionate amount is an unenforceable penalty; agreeing in advance on a fixed sum is the normal feature of such a clause.

q: A signed contract lists the wrong lot number because of a typing error, and both parties agree it does not reflect their actual deal. The remedy that corrects the document to match their true agreement is:
options: Rescission
Reformation
Novation
Specific performance
explanation: Reformation rewrites the document to match what the parties actually agreed when a mutual mistake in drafting occurred. Rescission would cancel the contract instead of fixing it.

q: The transfer of one party's rights under a contract to another person is called:
options: Delegation
Novation
Subordination
Assignment
explanation: Assignment transfers rights; delegation transfers duties. Neither releases the original party, which takes a novation.

q: A seller and buyer agree to cancel their existing contract and substitute a new one with a lower price and a later closing date, extinguishing the old contract entirely. This is:
options: An assignment
A ratification
A novation
A reformation
explanation: A novation replaces an old obligation with a new one, either between the same parties or by substituting a new party. Reformation only corrects a writing to reflect the original deal.

q: Which contract right is generally NOT assignable without the other party's consent?
options: A buyer's rights under a sale contract that is silent on assignment
A right to collect a sum of money already earned under a contract
A right to a personal service that depends on a particular person's skill
A seller's right to receive the balance due on a purchase-money note
explanation: Contracts for personal services rely on a specific person's skill or trust and cannot be shifted without consent. Rights to money and contract rights not restricted by a no-assignment clause are generally assignable.

q: A contract sets the closing 'on or about June 1' and does not say time is of the essence. The buyer is not ready on June 1 but can close June 10. Generally in New York:
options: The buyer is allowed a reasonable adjournment and is not yet in default
The buyer defaults on June 2 and forfeits the entire down payment
The contract automatically terminates at the end of June 1
The seller may immediately keep the deposit and resell the house
explanation: Without a time-of-the-essence clause, New York courts treat the closing date as a target, allowing a reasonable adjournment. A party in default is one who fails to perform within a reasonable time after that date.
citation: General contract law; New York case law on time of the essence

q: A contract states that time is of the essence for a June 1 closing. If the buyer cannot close on June 1, the buyer:
options: Gets an automatic 30-day extension
Has until the end of that week to close
May close at any time before the loan commitment expires
Is in material breach of the contract
explanation: A time-of-the-essence clause makes the exact date a strict condition, so failing to perform on that date is a material breach that can cost the defaulting party the deal and the deposit.

q: A contract has no time-of-the-essence clause, and the closing date has passed with the buyer stalling. The seller can generally make time of the essence by:
options: Immediately keeping the down payment once the original date passes
Giving clear written notice of a reasonable new date, warning that missing it is a default
Recording a notice of default in the county clerk's office
Asking the listing broker to cancel the contract on the seller's behalf
explanation: In New York, a party may make time of the essence after the fact by a clear, unequivocal notice that sets a reasonable date and states that failure to close then will be a default. Merely letting the original date pass does not create a default.
citation: General contract law; New York case law on time of the essence

q: A seller dies after signing a binding contract to sell her house but before closing. Generally:
options: The contract ends automatically at the seller's death
The contract binds her estate, which must complete the sale
The buyer must make a new offer to the seller's heirs
The contract becomes voidable by the seller's heirs
explanation: Death ends an unaccepted offer, but a binding contract to sell land survives and is enforceable against the seller's estate. Personal-service contracts, unlike land sales, may end on death.

q: Two months before closing, a seller emails the buyer, 'I will not sell to you under any circumstances.' The buyer:
options: Must wait until the closing date passes before suing
May treat this as an anticipatory breach and pursue remedies now
Has no remedy, because no performance is yet due
Must accept return of the deposit as the only remedy
explanation: A clear, unequivocal refusal to perform before the due date is an anticipatory repudiation, which lets the other party treat the contract as breached immediately and seek damages or specific performance.

q: A buyer with no mortgage contingency loses her job before closing and cannot get a loan. She claims the contract is discharged by impossibility. Generally:
options: Her financial hardship does not excuse her from performing
The contract is discharged because performance is impossible
The contract becomes voidable at her option
The contract is void because consideration failed
explanation: Impossibility requires that performance itself become objectively impossible, as when the subject property is destroyed. A party's personal inability to pay is not impossibility, and she assumed the financing risk by omitting a contingency.

q: Under the explanation that 19 NYCRR §175.24 requires on exclusive residential listings, what happens under an exclusive agency listing if another broker, not the listing broker, finds the buyer?
options: The owner owes a commission only to the broker who actually found the buyer
The owner owes a commission to both the selling broker and the listing broker
The owner owes no commission because the listing broker did not find the buyer
The owner owes one commission to the listing broker, who must share it by law
explanation: The DOS-mandated explanation warns that under an exclusive agency listing, if another broker finds a buyer, the owner will owe a commission to both the selling broker and the present broker. Only the owner's own sale escapes the commission; a sale by an outside broker does not.

q: A broker takes an exclusive right to sell listing on a two-family house. To comply with DOS rules, the required explanation of exclusive listing types must be:
options: read aloud to the owner at signing, with no signature or initials required
filed by the broker with the Department of State within ten days of signing
given to the owner only if the owner asks how the two listing types differ
printed on or attached to the listing and signed or initialed by the owner
explanation: Section 175.24(b) requires the explanation to be printed on or attached to the exclusive listing, in at least six-point type, and signed or initialed by the homeowner or the homeowner's agent. Reading it aloud does not satisfy the signature requirement, and nothing is filed with DOS.

q: Which of the following exclusive listings does NOT require the DOS explanation of exclusive right to sell versus exclusive agency?
options: A listing of a vacant lot on which the buyer plans to build a house
An exclusive agency listing of an owner-occupied condominium unit
An exclusive right to sell listing of a four-family dwelling
An exclusive right to sell listing of a cooperative apartment
explanation: Section 175.24 defines residential property as one-to-four family dwellings and condominium or cooperative apartments, and expressly excludes unimproved land on which such dwellings are to be built. A four-family house, a condo unit, and a co-op apartment are all covered, so only the vacant lot is outside the rule.

q: A broker who belongs to a multiple listing service takes an exclusive listing on a single-family home. DOS rules require the listing agreement to give the homeowner the option to:
options: keep the property out of the MLS for the first 30 days of the listing term
cancel the listing without penalty if no offer arrives within the first 60 days
have negotiated offers submitted through the listing broker or the selling broker
pay any cooperating broker directly instead of through the listing broker
explanation: Section 175.24(c) requires an MLS member's exclusive residential listing to let the homeowner choose whether negotiated offers are submitted through the listing broker or through the selling broker. The other choices describe terms the parties might negotiate, not a DOS requirement.

q: An exclusive right to sell listing expired March 31. It has a 90-day protection clause covering buyers shown the property during the term. On May 10, the owner, who has not relisted with anyone, sells directly to a buyer the listing salesperson showed the house to in February. The listing broker:
options: is owed nothing because the listing had already expired
is likely owed the commission under the protection clause
is owed only reimbursement of its advertising expenses
is owed a fee only if the buyer names that broker in writing
explanation: A protection (carryover or extension) clause makes the commission payable when, within the stated period after expiration, the owner sells to a buyer introduced during the listing term. The sale occurred 40 days after expiration to a buyer shown the home during the term, so the clause applies; expiration alone does not cut off the broker's claim.
citation: Listing agreement terms; general contract law

q: A salesperson obtains an exclusive right to sell listing, then transfers her license to a different brokerage before the house sells. The listing:
options: moves automatically to the salesperson's new sponsoring broker
ends on the day the salesperson's license transfer takes effect
becomes an open listing that any broker may now market freely
stays with the original broker, who remains the owner's agent
explanation: A listing is a contract between the owner and the broker; a salesperson acts only on behalf of the sponsoring broker. When the salesperson leaves, the listing stays with the original firm unless the owner and that broker agree otherwise.

q: Two weeks into a six-month exclusive right to sell listing, the sole owner dies. No contract of sale has been signed. The listing:
options: terminates by operation of law because the principal has died
continues for its full term and binds the owner's estate
converts to an exclusive agency listing for the executor
continues until the broker receives written notice of death
explanation: A listing creates an agency, and an agency ends automatically when the principal dies; notice to the broker is not required. The executor may sign a new listing, but the old one does not bind the estate.

q: A seller signs a contract of sale and dies a week before the scheduled closing. Generally:
options: the contract is void because one of its parties has since died
the buyer must either cancel or renegotiate the price with the heirs
the contract binds the seller's estate, which must convey to the buyer
the down payment must be refunded and the transaction started over
explanation: Unlike a listing, which is a personal-service agency that ends at death, a contract to sell real property survives the seller's death and binds the estate. The executor or administrator must perform and deliver the deed.

q: An owner's listing offers $480,000 cash with closing within 60 days and says the commission is earned when the broker produces a buyer on those terms. The broker produces a buyer ready, willing, and able to pay exactly that, but the owner changes her mind and refuses to sell. Generally, the broker:
options: has earned nothing because no contract of sale was signed
has likely earned the commission despite the owner's refusal
is owed half the commission as a cancellation fee by law
may sue only to force the owner to sell to that buyer
explanation: In New York, a broker generally earns the commission by producing a buyer ready, willing, and able to buy on the listing's terms, unless the agreement conditions payment on closing. The owner's change of heart does not defeat the claim, and the broker cannot force the sale itself.
citation: New York common law of brokerage commissions

q: A buyer's agent works under a written buyer agency agreement, but the agent's compensation will be paid out of the listing broker's commission, which the seller funds. Which statement is correct?
options: The buyer's agent becomes the seller's subagent by accepting the payment
The payment creates a dual agency that needs the seller's written consent
The buyer's agent must refuse the payment to avoid divided loyalty
The buyer's agent still owes fiduciary duties to the buyer, not the seller
explanation: Who pays the commission does not decide whom the agent represents; the agency relationship and its fiduciary duties come from the buyer agency agreement. Seller-funded compensation is common and does not make the buyer's agent a subagent or a dual agent.

q: A buyer signs an exclusive buyer agency agreement stating that the broker is paid if the buyer buys any home of the described type during the term, no matter who finds it. The buyer locates a for-sale-by-owner house herself and buys it during the term. Under these terms:
options: the buyer's broker is likely owed the agreed compensation
the buyer's broker is owed nothing because no listing existed
the for-sale-by-owner seller must pay the buyer broker's fee
the agreement is void because it limits the buyer's choices
explanation: This agreement works like an exclusive right to sell listing on the buyer side: the trigger is the buyer's purchase during the term, regardless of who locates the property. The seller never agreed to pay, so the buyer bears the fee under her own contract.
citation: Buyer agency agreement terms; general contract law

q: Both parties sign a binder stating the sale is "subject to a formal contract to be prepared by the seller's attorney," and the buyer leaves a small good-faith deposit. Before any contract is signed, the seller accepts a higher offer. Generally:
options: the seller is in breach and must convey the house to the first buyer
the seller must pay the first buyer the difference between the two prices
the seller may do so because the binder called for a later formal contract
the binder became a binding contract once the deposit was accepted
explanation: A binder that expressly makes the deal subject to a formal contract shows the parties did not intend to be bound until that contract is signed, so either side may withdraw before then. Accepting a deposit does not by itself turn the binder into an enforceable contract of sale.
citation: GOL §5-703; New York contract law on agreements to agree

q: A binder is most likely to be enforceable as a contract of sale when it:
options: is accompanied by a good-faith deposit delivered to the listing broker
is signed and states all essential terms without reserving a formal contract
has been reviewed and initialed on each page by the buyer's salesperson
is later recorded by the listing broker in the county clerk's office
explanation: A binder can be a binding contract if it is a signed writing containing all essential terms and the parties did not condition their deal on a later formal contract. A deposit, a salesperson's initials, or recording does not supply the missing intent or terms.

q: A salesperson filling out a binder writes in her own clause making the seller liable for any future problem with an unpermitted deck. Under New York law, this is best described as:
options: acceptable, because licensees may write any clause both parties approve
acceptable, as long as the sponsoring broker reviews the clause first
acceptable only when the salesperson represents the seller, not the buyer
drafting a legal provision, which risks the unauthorized practice of law
explanation: Licensees may fill in factual blanks on a form, such as names, price, and dates, but composing clauses that allocate legal rights is the practice of law. New York courts have disciplined brokers for drafting contract provisions, and party approval or broker review does not cure it.
citation: Judiciary Law §478; Duncan & Hill Realty v. Department of State (App. Div. 1978)

q: In typical downstate (New York City area) practice, which sequence usually follows an accepted offer?
options: Seller's attorney drafts; buyer signs and pays the down payment; seller signs and delivers
Listing broker drafts; both parties sign at the showing; attorneys review it at closing
Buyer's attorney drafts; seller signs first; buyer pays the down payment at closing
Title company drafts; lender signs first; both parties sign it at the closing table
explanation: Downstate, the seller's attorney customarily prepares the contract; the buyer signs first and delivers the down payment, and the deal binds once the seller signs and the contract is delivered. Brokers do not draft these contracts, and the down payment comes at contract signing, not at closing.

q: An upstate contract includes a standard attorney approval contingency. The buyer has second thoughts and tells her attorney to disapprove, and the attorney sends a timely written disapproval giving no reason. The result is:
options: the buyer is bound, because buyer's remorse is not a valid ground
the disapproval is void unless it identifies a specific legal defect
the contract ends, because disapproval may rest on any reason or none
the seller may keep the deposit as liquidated damages for bad faith
explanation: New York's highest court held that an unrestricted attorney approval clause lets the attorney disapprove for any reason or no reason, even when the client simply changed her mind. Courts will not probe the motive, so a timely disapproval ends the contract.

q: Why do upstate purchase contracts prepared by licensees on a standard form commonly include an attorney approval contingency?
options: It lets the listing broker extend the listing period until the attorneys meet
Each party's lawyer can review terms set by non-lawyers before they become binding
It replaces the need for a separate mortgage commitment contingency clause
It gives the buyer's lender the right to rewrite the agreed purchase price
explanation: Because a licensee, not a lawyer, fills in the form, the attorney approval clause gives each side's attorney a short window to review and disapprove before the contract becomes firm. It does not substitute for financing protection or affect the listing.
citation: Upstate contract practice; Moran v. Erk, 11 N.Y.3d 452 (2008)

q: A contract's attorney approval clause allows written disapproval within three business days after full execution, excluding weekends and holidays. The contract is fully executed on a Thursday, and no holidays intervene. The last day for disapproval is the following:
options: Sunday
Monday
Wednesday
Tuesday
explanation: Counting starts the day after execution and skips the weekend: Friday is day 1, Monday is day 2, Tuesday is day 3. Sunday comes from counting calendar days (Fri, Sat, Sun); Monday comes from wrongly counting Thursday itself as day 1.
citation: Contract terms; Moran v. Erk, 11 N.Y.3d 452 (2008)

q: A contract has a mortgage commitment contingency, but the buyer never submits a loan application. On the commitment date, she claims no commitment was issued and demands her down payment back. Most likely, the buyer:
options: cannot rely on the contingency because she did not apply in good faith
gets the deposit back because no commitment was issued by the date
gets half the deposit back under the default rule for split deposits
may extend the commitment date on her own by another thirty days
explanation: A mortgage contingency requires the buyer to apply promptly and pursue the loan diligently and in good faith. A buyer who causes the condition to fail by never applying cannot use it to escape, so she risks being in default.
citation: General contract law (implied good faith; prevention doctrine)

q: A contract is contingent on the buyer obtaining a commitment for a $400,000 loan. The lender issues a commitment for only $340,000. Generally, the buyer:
options: must accept the smaller loan and bring the shortfall in cash to the closing
is in default because the lender issued a commitment before the deadline
may treat the contingency as unmet because the loan is below the contract amount
must keep reapplying with the same lender until the full amount is approved
explanation: The contingency is satisfied only by a commitment meeting the contract's terms. A $340,000 commitment is $60,000 short of the $400,000 specified, so the buyer may rely on the contingency rather than make up the difference.

q: A contract says that if the buyer has not obtained a mortgage commitment by the commitment date, the buyer must notify the seller in writing by that date or the contingency is waived. The buyer sends no notice, and her loan is denied two weeks later. Most likely:
options: the buyer may still cancel because the lender made the final decision
the contingency was waived, and the buyer's down payment is at risk
the seller must extend the commitment date for another thirty days
the contract becomes an all-cash deal with no deposit at risk
explanation: Contingencies protect the buyer only if she follows their notice procedures and deadlines. Here the contract deems the contingency waived when no timely notice is given, so a later denial leaves the buyer bound and her deposit exposed.

q: A contract's mortgage contingency exists solely for the buyer's benefit. The buyer decides to pay cash and notifies the seller that she waives the contingency. The seller, seeing prices rise, wants out. Generally:
options: the seller may cancel because a contract term has been altered
the waiver is ineffective until the seller signs it as well
the waiver is ineffective until the lender confirms it in writing
the buyer may waive it, and the seller remains bound to sell
explanation: A party may waive a condition that exists only for that party's benefit, and the other party stays bound. The seller cannot treat the buyer's waiver as a modification that frees the seller.

q: A contract gives the buyer ten days to deliver written notice that the home inspection is unsatisfactory. The inspector flags an aging roof, but the buyer sends nothing until day 14. Generally:
options: the contingency has lapsed, so the buyer remains bound to the contract
the buyer may still cancel because the roof defect is material
the seller must replace the roof before the buyer has to close
the inspection period restarts when the written report arrives
explanation: An inspection contingency must be exercised within its stated period and in the required form. Notice on day 14 misses the ten-day window, so the contingency is treated as satisfied or waived and the buyer stays bound.

q: A purchase contract is contingent on the sale of the buyer's current home and includes a 72-hour kick-out clause. The seller receives an acceptable backup offer. Under the clause, the seller:
options: may cancel at once without giving the first buyer any notice or chance to act
can require the first buyer to close within 72 hours or forfeit the deposit
notifies the buyer, who has 72 hours to remove the contingency or lose the deal
must make the backup buyer wait until the first buyer's home actually sells
explanation: A kick-out (escape) clause lets the seller keep marketing; when a backup offer arrives, the seller gives notice and the first buyer must waive the sale-of-home contingency within the stated time or the seller may cancel. It does not force the first buyer to close in 72 hours.

q: A downstate contract sets a $685,000 price with a 10% down payment due at contract signing. The buyer already gave a $5,000 binder deposit that the contract credits toward the down payment. How much must the buyer pay at contract signing?
explanation: Down payment = $685,000 × 10% = $68,500; less the $5,000 credit = $63,500 due at signing. $68,500 ignores the credit; $68,000 and $63,000 come from wrongly subtracting the deposit from the price before taking 10% (($685,000 − $5,000) × 10% = $68,000).

q: The buyer cancels, citing the mortgage contingency; the seller says the buyer defaulted. Both demand the down payment held by the seller's attorney as escrowee. The escrowee should generally:
options: release the funds to the seller, because the escrowee is the seller's attorney
split the funds equally between the parties and close the escrow
return the funds to the buyer, because the buyer deposited them
hold the funds until joint written instructions or a court order
explanation: An escrowee is a neutral stakeholder bound by the escrow terms. When the parties dispute who is entitled to the down payment, the escrowee keeps it until both parties agree in writing or a court decides; the escrowee's relationship with the seller does not let it pick a side.
citation: Escrow terms of the contract; general escrow law

q: A $540,000 contract calls for a 10% down payment at signing, held in escrow and credited at closing, and an 80% mortgage. Ignoring closing costs and adjustments, how much more cash must the buyer bring to closing?
explanation: Down payment = $540,000 × 10% = $54,000; loan = $540,000 × 80% = $432,000. Cash at closing = $540,000 − $54,000 − $432,000 = $54,000. $108,000 forgets to credit the escrowed down payment; $43,200 is 10% of the loan; $0 counts the down payment twice.

q: An owner grants a six-month option to buy her house for $410,000 in exchange for $6,000. Two months later she gets a $450,000 offer and wants to revoke the option. Generally, she:
options: may revoke by refunding the $6,000 option fee to the optionee
may revoke because the optionee never promised to buy the house
cannot revoke; the optionee may still buy at $410,000 during the term
must let the optionee match the $450,000 offer or lose the right
explanation: Because the optionee paid consideration, the owner's offer is irrevocable for the option period, and the optionee may buy at the fixed $410,000 price. Requiring a match of a third-party offer describes a right of first refusal, not an option.

q: An optionee lets a purchase option expire without exercising it. Usually:
options: the optionee owes the full purchase price as damages
the optionor keeps the option money and may sell to anyone
the optionor must refund the option money to the optionee
the optionee has breached a bilateral contract of sale
explanation: An option binds only the optionor; the optionee has the choice, not a duty, to buy. If the option lapses, the optionor keeps the consideration paid for holding the offer open and is free to sell elsewhere.

q: A tenant's lease gives her a right of first refusal. The owner receives a bona fide $600,000 offer she wants to accept. Generally, the owner must:
options: sell to the tenant at a price set by an independent appraiser
accept the offer and notify the tenant after the sale closes
let the tenant buy at the price stated in the original lease
offer the tenant a chance to buy on the same terms before accepting
explanation: A right of first refusal is triggered when the owner decides to sell and receives an acceptable third-party offer; the holder may then match those terms. Unlike an option, it fixes no price in advance, so a lease-stated price is not the measure.
citation: General contract law (rights of first refusal)

q: A tenant with a right of first refusal declines to match a $600,000 offer. That deal collapses, and months later the owner sells to someone else for $540,000 without telling the tenant. Most likely:
options: the owner had to re-offer the property to the tenant at the lower price
the tenant's right ended permanently once she declined the first offer
no re-offer was needed because a lower price only benefits the tenant
the tenant may now demand the property at the earlier $600,000 price
explanation: Declining one offer generally does not let the owner sell later on materially different, more favorable terms without giving the holder a new chance to match. A $60,000 price cut ($600,000 − $540,000) is a material change, so the tenant should have been offered the $540,000 deal.
citation: General contract law (rights of first refusal)

q: A lease-option tenant paid an $8,000 option fee credited toward a $350,000 purchase price and receives a $200 rent credit for each of 12 months. She exercises after 12 months. How much of the price remains?
explanation: Rent credits = $200 × 12 = $2,400. Remaining = $350,000 − $8,000 − $2,400 = $339,600. $342,000 omits the rent credits, $347,600 omits the option fee, and $337,200 counts the rent credits twice.

q: During an installment land contract, the buyer usually:
options: holds legal title, while the seller holds a purchase-money mortgage
has possession and equitable title, while the seller keeps legal title
has no interest in the land at all until the final payment is made
shares legal title with the seller as a tenant in common until paid
explanation: Under a land (installment) contract the vendee takes possession and equitable title and pays over time; the vendor delivers the deed, and legal title, only when the contract is paid as agreed. If legal title passed with a mortgage back, it would be a purchase-money mortgage sale instead.
citation: General real property law (installment land contracts)

q: A land contract vendee has paid more than half the price over several years and improved the property, then defaults. The vendor wants to declare a forfeiture, keep every payment, and simply evict. In New York:
options: the vendor may simply retake possession and keep every payment received
the vendee automatically receives a deed to a share matching the payments
the contract converts into a lease and the payments are treated as rent
a court may require the vendor to foreclose the vendee's equitable interest
explanation: New York courts treat a vendee who has paid a substantial part of the price as holding an equitable interest like a mortgagor's, so the vendor may be required to foreclose rather than declare a forfeiture. That protects the vendee's equity, including any surplus from a sale.

q: How can a land contract vendee best protect against the vendor later selling or mortgaging the property to someone else?
options: Record the contract or a memorandum of it with the county clerk
Keep the canceled checks for every installment payment made
Post a written notice of the contract on the property itself
File a copy of the contract with the Department of State
explanation: New York permits an executory contract for the sale of real property to be recorded, which gives constructive notice to later purchasers and lenders. Payment records and posted notices do not give record notice, and DOS does not record land documents.

q: Before closing, while the seller still has both title and possession, a fire not caused by the buyer destroys a material part of the house. The contract is silent on risk of loss. The buyer:
options: must close at the full price and collect from the seller's insurer
must close but may deduct the fire damage from the purchase price
may cancel and recover the down payment, since the seller cannot enforce
loses the deposit because equitable title passed when she signed
explanation: Under the Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act, when neither title nor possession has passed and a material part is destroyed without the purchaser's fault, the vendor cannot enforce the contract and the purchaser may recover what she paid. The common-law equitable-conversion rule that put risk on the buyer does not apply.

q: Before closing, with title and possession still in the seller, a storm destroys a small detached shed of minor value. Nothing else is damaged. Under the Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act:
options: the buyer may cancel and recover the entire down payment
the contract remains enforceable, with a price abatement for the loss
the buyer must close at the full price with no reduction
the seller may cancel because the property has changed
explanation: When only an immaterial part is destroyed before title or possession passes, neither party may escape the contract, but the price is abated to the extent of the loss. Cancellation is available only when a material part is destroyed.

q: By agreement, the buyer moves in two weeks before closing. A storm then badly damages the house through no fault of the seller. The contract is silent on risk of loss. Generally:
options: the seller bears the loss because the deed had not yet been delivered
the buyer may cancel because a material part of the house was damaged
the price is reduced by the cost of repairing the storm damage
the buyer must still pay the full price because possession had passed
explanation: Under GOL §5-1311, once either legal title or possession has passed to the purchaser, destruction without the vendor's fault does not relieve the purchaser of the duty to pay or entitle her to a refund. Early possession therefore shifts the risk to the buyer.

q: Before title or possession passes, the state takes most of the property by eminent domain. Under the Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act, generally:
options: the seller cannot enforce the contract, and the buyer may recover the deposit
the act covers only fire damage, so ordinary contract rules apply instead
the buyer must close because the taking was not caused by the seller
the buyer must close and take the condemnation award as the property
explanation: GOL §5-1311 treats a taking by eminent domain of all or a material part like destruction: if neither title nor possession has passed, the vendor cannot enforce the contract and the purchaser may recover what she has paid. The act is not limited to fire.

q: Which statement about New York's Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act is accurate?
options: It shifts the risk of loss to the buyer once the contract is signed
It applies only to sales of commercial and investment property
Its risk rules apply unless the contract expressly provides otherwise
Its rules cannot be changed by any term of the parties' contract
explanation: GOL §5-1311 is a default rule: it governs unless the contract expressly allocates risk differently, which many attorney-drafted contracts do. It keeps risk on the seller until title or possession passes, rather than shifting it at signing.

q: A contract sets closing "on or about June 1" and does not say time is of the essence. The buyer's lender is slow, and the buyer is ready June 9. On June 2 the seller declares the buyer in default. Generally, the seller:
options: may cancel because the buyer missed the agreed closing date
likely cannot cancel, because the date was not made of the essence
may keep the deposit as liquidated damages for the delay
may charge the buyer a per-diem penalty fixed by state law
explanation: In New York, a closing date that is not made of the essence is a target date; either party is entitled to a reasonable adjournment. A one-day delay is not a default, so the seller cannot cancel or keep the deposit.
citation: New York case law on time of the essence

q: When a contract does not make time of the essence, a party may later make it so by notice. To be effective, that notice generally must:
options: be given orally at least one business day before the new closing date
be approved by the Department of State before it is served on the party
set any date the sender chooses, no matter how short the time allowed
be clear, set a reasonable date, and warn that failing to close is a default
explanation: New York courts require a time-of-the-essence notice to be clear and unequivocal, to fix a reasonable time to perform, and to warn that failure to perform by then will be treated as a default. An unreasonably short deadline is ineffective, and DOS plays no role.
citation: New York case law on time of the essence

q: A contract states that the March 15 closing date is "time of the essence." The seller is ready to close, but the buyer is not and asks for one more week. Generally:
options: the buyer is in default, and the seller may pursue contract remedies
the buyer gets a reasonable adjournment as a matter of law
the seller must grant one 30-day extension before declaring default
the clause is unenforceable in residential home sales
explanation: When time is of the essence, the stated date is firm: a party who cannot perform on that date is in default, and the ready party may cancel and pursue its remedies. The reasonable-adjournment rule applies only when time is not of the essence.
citation: New York case law on time of the essence

q: A seller serves a proper time-of-the-essence notice setting July 20 for closing. On July 20 the seller cannot deliver clear title because of an unpaid judgment lien, and the buyer does not appear. Generally, the seller:
options: may keep the deposit because the buyer failed to appear on the date
may cancel because the notice made the July 20 date of the essence
cannot hold the buyer in default, because the seller was not ready either
may move the closing date alone and hold the buyer to the new date
explanation: A party who declares the other in default on a time-of-the-essence date must itself be ready, willing, and able to perform on that date. An unpaid judgment lien means the seller could not deliver the title required, so the seller cannot cancel or keep the deposit.
citation: New York case law on time of the essence

q: A contract of sale says nothing about assignment. Before closing, the buyer assigns her rights to her wholly owned LLC. Generally, the assignment is:
options: void unless the seller consents in writing
valid even without the seller's consent
valid only if the LLC pays a new deposit
valid only after the contract is redrafted
explanation: A real estate purchase contract is generally assignable unless it prohibits assignment, so the LLC may take the buyer's place. The buyer as assignor stays liable unless the seller agrees to release her through a novation.

q: A contract states that the buyer may not assign it without the seller's prior written consent. The buyer assigns it to a cousin anyway, and the seller objects. Generally:
options: the seller must accept because sale contracts are assignable
the seller must accept if the cousin can pay all cash
the clause is void as an unlawful restraint on sale
the seller may refuse to close with the cousin
explanation: Parties may contract to bar assignment, and an anti-assignment clause requiring consent is enforceable. Without consent, the seller need not deal with the assignee; the general rule of assignability applies only when the contract is silent.

q: A tenant has two years left on a three-year lease when the owner sells the building. Generally:
options: the new owner takes title subject to the lease for its remaining term
the lease ends automatically when title passes to the new owner
the new owner may end the lease on 30 days' written notice
the tenant must sign a new lease with the new owner to stay
explanation: A lease is both a conveyance of possession and a contract, and a sale of the building does not end it. The buyer steps into the landlord's position and is bound by the lease for the rest of its term unless the lease says otherwise.

q: A fire not caused by the tenant makes an apartment untenantable. The lease says nothing about fire damage. Under New York law, the tenant:
options: must keep paying rent until the lease term expires
must stay and wait until the landlord completes repairs
may quit and surrender possession and owe no further rent
may withhold rent but must remain in possession
explanation: When leased premises are destroyed or made untenantable by fire or the elements without the tenant's fault, and there is no agreement to the contrary, the tenant may quit and surrender possession and is not liable for rent afterward.

q: A lease automatically renews for another year unless the tenant gives notice 60 days before it expires. The landlord never reminds the tenant of this clause, and the tenant moves out when the term ends. Under New York law:
options: the lease renews automatically for another full year
the renewal clause cannot be enforced against the tenant
the tenant owes rent for the missed 60-day notice period
the renewal binds the tenant because she signed the lease
explanation: GOL §5-905 makes an automatic renewal clause inoperative unless the landlord gives the tenant written notice of it 15 to 30 days before the tenant's notice deadline. Without that reminder, the tenant may leave at the end of the term.
